analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Clean Air Act rules phasing out chemicals that destroy the ozone layer.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in October 1994, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Tom DeLay introduced a bill to wipe out Title VI of the Clean Air Act, the section that requires phasing out chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other chemicals that eat away at the Earth's ozone layer — the shield that blocks the sun's most cancer-causing ultraviolet rays. If it had passed, chemical makers and other businesses that use or sell ozone-depleting chemicals would have been freed from the phaseout schedule. Instead, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, manufacturers and users of ozone-depleting chemicals — makers of CFC refrigerants, foam-blowing agents, and aerosol propellants, and the companies still depending on them — would have been released from phaseout deadlines and the cost of switching to safer substitutes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Title VI of the Clean Air Act in its entirety, eliminating all federal requirements for protecting stratospheric ozone, including the phaseout of CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through increased exposure to ultraviolet radiation as ozone depletion continued — raising the risk of skin cancer and cataracts — while the phaseout of dangerous chemicals stopped and safer substitutes lost their legal push.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to rising UV radiation

drawbacks.text: The public health cost would have been large: ozone-depleting chemicals are the direct cause of thinning the ozone layer, and the Clean Air Act's Title VI rules exist to prevent additional skin cancers and cataracts by ending those emissions [S3].

Repealing Title VI would have pulled federal law out of line with the international Montreal Protocol, the treaty under which the United States and other nations agreed to phase out CFCs, creating conflict with trade and treaty obligations [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have saved chemical producers and CFC users the cost of complying with the phaseout, but only by reversing the federal rules that prevent ozone depletion — a trade of concentrated cost savings for a public health harm spread across everyone. It never came close to enactment: it had a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and died without even a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative Tom DeLay introduced the bill on October 6, 1994, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No industry gained anything, because the bill died before any vote; the ozone-protection rules stayed on the books, and the public was spared the repeal of chemical phaseout requirements. The outcome favored ordinary people only in the sense that a bill that would have weakened their health protections never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died in committee

for.name: Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act's stratospheric ozone protection provisions [S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action — never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote — after the bill was referred [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors, so no partisan or cross-party support was recorded.

industries.note: Repealing Title VI would have canceled the mandatory phaseout of ozone-depleting chemicals, letting producers keep selling products the law was phasing out at the cost of continued ozone depletion and higher public UV exposure.

industries.industry: Aerosol, foam, and refrigeration businesses still using CFCs
industries.note: These users would have avoided the cost of converting to safer substitutes, but many had already invested in the transition, so the gain would have gone mainly to the laggards while undermining the substitute market.

industries.industry: Producers of CFC substitutes and ozone-safe refrigerants
industries.note: Repeal would have removed the legal force behind demand for safer alternatives, cutting into the market for replacement chemicals.
